title: Distributed Unique ID Generator
oneLine: Generate sortable 64-bit IDs locally by packing timestamp, location, worker, and per-millisecond sequence bits—with explicit clock-drift handling.
opening: My default is a Snowflake-style 64-bit identifier because it avoids a central database call while remaining roughly time ordered and index friendly. I allocate bits to a custom epoch timestamp, datacenter, worker, and sequence counter. Each worker generates IDs locally and can issue several thousand IDs per millisecond. Worker IDs come from a leased, fenced registry so two live workers never share an identity. The main operational risk is clock rollback: the generator should use a monotonic clock where possible, wait for small rollback, switch to a reserved clock/epoch bit or stop for unsafe rollback, and alert. I would make the bit layout configurable only through a controlled compatibility plan because it determines lifetime and capacity.
ask: Must IDs be numeric, URL-safe, opaque, sortable, or globally unique?
What generation rate and lifetime are required?
Can clients infer creation time or business volume?
Are IDs generated in multiple regions while disconnected?

nonFunctional: Operational safety under clock or worker failure

scale: A 12-bit sequence supports 4,096 IDs per worker per millisecond.
10 worker bits allow 1,024 worker identities; split between region/datacenter and machine as needed.
41 timestamp bits at millisecond precision last about 69 years from the custom epoch.

decisions.default: Snowflake for database/index locality and compact numeric IDs; UUIDv7 when standards/interoperability and decentralized generation matter.
decisions.why: Random UUIDs fragment ordered indexes; time-ordered UUIDs reduce that cost.
decisions.switch: Use random/opaque IDs when timestamp leakage or enumeration is a security concern.

decisions.default: Avoid it on the critical path unless strict monotonic sequence is required.
decisions.why: It is simple but becomes a coordination and availability bottleneck.
decisions.switch: Allocate ID ranges in batches from a central service to combine monotonic blocks with local generation.

decisions.default: Fence worker IDs, detect rollback, wait for small skew, and halt or use a logical epoch for large skew.
decisions.switch: Use consensus-backed sequence ranges when physical time cannot be trusted.

deepDives.title: Bit allocation
points: Start from required lifetime, nodes, and per-node burst—not a memorized layout.
Reserve room for future region growth or use a namespace/version bit.
Document signed/unsigned behavior across Java, JavaScript, and databases.

deepDives.title: Worker identity
points: Lease IDs from etcd/ZooKeeper with session expiry.
Use fencing tokens so an old process cannot resume after its lease was reassigned.
Persist last timestamp across restart when needed.

failures.response: Leased worker registry, fencing token, and startup refusal on duplicate ownership.
Detect against last timestamp, wait/quarantine, use logical offset, and alert; never silently reset sequence.
Wait for next tick, increase sequence bits, or distribute load across more workers.
Encode/obfuscate externally, use UUIDv7/random public IDs, or separate internal and public identifiers.

questions.q: Are Snowflake IDs strictly ordered globally?
questions.a: They are roughly time ordered, not a single global sequence. Clock differences and concurrent workers mean two IDs can be generated in a different order than their numeric value.
It is simple for one database, but multi-primary allocation, failover, and a central write hotspot complicate global scale. It is still the right answer for many modest systems.

questions.q: What happens after the timestamp field expires?
questions.a: The bit layout needs a migration/version plan long before expiry—new namespace, wider ID, or a new epoch distinguished by version. This is a compatibility concern across every consumer.

questions.q: How do you expose IDs to JavaScript?
questions.a: A 64-bit integer exceeds JavaScript’s safe Number range. Return it as a string or BigInt-compatible representation and keep schemas consistent.

mistakes: Ignoring NTP rollback and VM clock behavior
Memorizing a bit layout without deriving capacity
seniorSignal: Derive the layout from lifetime and throughput, then spend most of the discussion on identity leases, fencing, clock failure, public-information leakage, and migration.
implementation: Java long with bit shifts; return as a string over JSON
Worker leases and fencing in etcd/ZooKeeper
Micrometer metrics for rollback, sequence wait, lease renewal, and generation rate
Consider UUIDv7 for interoperable time-ordered public IDs
